tier_reason: RESULTS-macos-apple-m3-pro-11c.md is a head-to-head against SQLite 3.45.0 (bundled via rusqlite), PostgreSQL 16.14 and Turso 0.7.0, produced by the public harness crates/mpedb-bench/src (h2h.rs, eng_sqlite.rs, workloads.rs; `cargo run --release -p mpedb-bench`). The page states the compiler (rustc 1.96.0), the flags (--release, lto=thin; the workspace [profile.release] also sets codegen-units=1) and the CPU (Apple M3 Pro, 11 cores), so all A criteria are met.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Apple M3 Pro page: point-select (tmpfs, none-class) mpedb 1,975,698 vs SQLite 320,201 ops/s (~6.2x, derived from page data). Point-select (disk, commit-class, mpedb durability=wal vs SQLite sync=FULL+WAL) 1,942,515 vs 762,437 (~2.5x, derived from page data). Point-insert (tmpfs, none-class) 230,660 vs 115,491 ops/s (~2.0x, derived from page data). Contended-writes (4 threads, tmpfs, none-class) 147,059 vs 102,066 (~1.4x, derived from page data). Separate Linux run (RESULTS-linux-amd-epyc-milan-2c.md, AMD EPYC-Milan 2 cores, tmpfs none-class): point-select 490,310 vs SQLite 79,619 ops/s (~6.2x, derived from page data). Durable single-client writes are roughly a tie on the M3.
corrections.workload: 50,000-row seeded table per cell. Cells: point-insert, point-select, point-update, 4-thread contended-writes and 3-reader+1-writer read-while-write. Each runs in a none-class mode (tmpfs, no fsync) and a commit-class mode (real disk, durable-on-ack; mpedb commit and wal vs SQLite sync=FULL+WAL), plus a durability-class table for single-client durable inserts. The same harness was re-run separately on a 2-core AMD EPYC-Milan Linux VM (tmpfs=/dev/shm, disk=xfs), published as RESULTS-linux-amd-epyc-milan-2c.md.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.96.0 (ac68faa20 2026-05-25) on macOS and rustc 1.96.1 on the Linux run; --release with workspace [profile.release] lto=thin, codegen-units=1. SQLite is the rusqlite 0.31 bundled 3.45.0 build, compiled by the same toolchain.
corrections.caveats: The license is NOT OSI-approved. It is the custom 'mpedb License 1.0': free for everyone except a one-time USD 0.07/device fee for groups with more than $5B revenue or valuation. The code can be used and studied, but it is not plain permissive open source. The benchmark was run on mpedb 0.1.0 and releases are now at 0.2.1. It is a single run on one machine with no confidence intervals, and the author says to treat differences under 20% as noise. mpedb does not win every cell. On the M3, SQLite is faster at durable point-update (392 vs 300 ops/s for mpedb wal), at single-client durable insert (353 vs 328), and at 4.4x in the crash-consistent-deferred class (86,062 vs 19,720 ops/s). The SQLite none-class baseline is journal_mode=MEMORY + synchronous=OFF. The author is careful about methodology: durability classes are kept separate, F_FULLFSYNC is forced on macOS, and the page states that every cell is reported, including the ones mpedb loses.

notes: The record's 'volume-backed re-run' numbers (490,310 vs 79,619) do not come from the M3 page. They are the tmpfs point-select cell of the separate Linux EPYC-Milan 2-core results file, so the label is fixed. All other M3 numbers match exactly. The commits API gives 2026-08-28 as the last commit on main (pushed_at is 2026-09-01). Metadata checks out: 11 stars, not a fork, not archived, spdx NOASSERTION with the custom license confirmed.

tier_reason: The README Benchmarks table compares against fjall 2.11.2 and redb 2.6.3 using the public harness benchmarks/main.rs (plus engine.rs, workloads.rs, protocol.rs). It states rustc 1.88.0 and the Apple M4 (Mac16,1). The optimization flags are in the committed benchmarks/Cargo.toml [profile.bench] (opt-level=3, lto=thin, codegen-units=1), and the raw JSON/TXT artifacts pin the commit. So A holds; the downgrade is for the overstated claim, not the tier.

corrections.baseline: fjall (the page's like-for-like peer); redb shown only as architectural context
corrections.claimed_speedup: Like-for-like vs fjall (TurboKV Durable vs fjall Buffer, both process-crash-recoverable, no per-write sync): sequential fill 1,774,574 vs 485,252 ops/s (~3.7x, derived from page data); random fill 906,806 vs 456,924 (~2.0x, derived from page data); batch 1,000/txn 2,380,390 vs 572,671 (~4.2x, derived from page data). The TurboKV column comes from a separate 'modes' run; in the single ingest run the ratios are ~1.8-4.4x (derived from page data). Against redb there is no like-for-like number, because redb Eventual issues a macOS F_BARRIERFSYNC per transaction. TurboKV Fast (no WAL) batch-1000 at 3,724,635 vs redb 134,636 (~27.7x, derived from page data) crosses durability classes, and the page says Fast 'is not comparable to persistent engine rows'. TurboKV Paranoid (full sync) loses to redb Eventual at 1 key/txn (213 vs 1,397) and at 100 keys/txn (20,670 vs 80,197), and edges it at 1,000 keys/txn (162,938 vs 134,636).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.88.0 (6b00bc388 2025-06-23); cargo bench with benchmarks/Cargo.toml [profile.bench] opt-level=3, lto=thin, codegen-units=1. The README recommends RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+aes,+neon (ARM) / +aes,+sse2 (x86) for the AES Bloom-filter path, but the result artifacts do not record RUSTFLAGS.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark, though the methodology is unusually complete (pinned versions, source-manifest hash, raw repetitions, CVs). The author compares cross-engine only against fjall and treats redb as 'architectural context'. The artifacts themselves say 'These are baseline observations, not performance claims.' The README table mixes two runs: the TurboKV columns come from the modes artifact and the fjall/redb columns from an earlier ingest artifact. The redb write gap is mostly a durability-boundary artifact (a per-transaction macOS barrier fsync). In the older TurboKV 0.5.0 full matrix, redb beats TurboKV on random reads (246,119 vs 183,154 ops/s), recovery and compaction, and ties on sequential scans. Only writes were benchmarked in the current table. Single machine (Apple M4, APFS), OS page cache not cleared.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly, but the record's headline (~27x vs redb) pits TurboKV Fast (no WAL) against redb's barrier-synced Eventual mode, which the page explicitly calls not comparable. So claimed_speedup is restated around the fjall like-for-like rows, and baseline is changed to fjall with redb as context. Metadata verified: Apache-2.0, 270 stars, last commit 2026-08-29, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: The NuGet README ('Fast Benchmark (2025)') gives first-party SQLite-vs-BTreePlus Pro timings (4M: 4.53 s vs 1.03 s; 1B: 2410 s vs 346 s) and the PostgreSQL WAL comparison. It gives no benchmark code, no SQLite configuration and no CPU for the SQLite table. The GitHub repo and the documentation PDF contain no SQLite benchmark harness either, so C stands.

corrections.license: MIT for the Community Edition NuGet package (binary only) and the demo/docs repo; the engine source is not published; the Pro/Enterprise Edition is proprietary (private NuGet feed plus license token)
corrections.caveats: The engine is binary-only. NOTICE.md says 'Engine source code is not included in this repository'; the GitHub repo holds only docs, a demo Program.cs and a csproj that references the NuGet package. The headline SQLite and PostgreSQL numbers use the closed, paid Pro Edition (page cache plus Bulk Insert, both of which Community lacks). The Community Edition runs with the cache off, which the vendor PDF puts at ~418K inserts/s vs ~3.16M with the cache on. The GitHub README credits the Community Edition with '3M inserts 0.95 s vs SQLite (WAL) 3.10 s (~3.26x)', which conflicts with those PDF figures. The SQLite table gives no CPU, SQLite pragmas or transaction batching; the PostgreSQL table gives i9-13900 + Samsung 990 PRO. The ~16% vs PostgreSQL is a time reduction (6m08s vs 5m10s, ~1.19x throughput). Only 9 GitHub stars (NuGet: ~11.8K downloads).

notes: The numbers match the NuGet page exactly, and the record correctly notes that the SQLite comparison gives no CPU. The main fix is has_code=false: no engine source exists publicly, only an MIT-licensed binary. Metadata verified: repo license MIT, 9 stars, last commit 2026-01-23, not a fork, not archived.
